title: I Become a Student
subtitle: How independent study turns received knowledge into a question worth pursuing

stages.title: Introduction · A possibility, with conditions

nodes.label: The claim
nodes.text: A real university education is possible, though rare. Students need the [[capacity and drive]] to learn.

nodes.label: The condition
nodes.text: Pursue [[methodical, independent study]] while resisting institutional [[mind-fixing]].

stages.title: The method · Choose a direction and develop the tools

nodes.label: Direction
nodes.text: [[Interest-driven specialization]] gives deep independent study its focus.

nodes.label: Reading and memory
nodes.text: Read extensively. Practise [[selective memorization]] grounded in understanding.

nodes.label: Critical thinking
nodes.text: Bring ideas from other disciplines to bear on historical questions.

stages.title: The method · Let disagreement become a question
stages.relation: use these habits to examine accounts

nodes.label: Find a starting point
nodes.text: Use authoritative references and ask professors for further reading.

nodes.label: Compare accounts
nodes.text: Look for [[conflicting claims]] about the same historical events.

nodes.label: Check other authorities
nodes.text: Consult libraries and professors for [[triangulation]].

stages.title: The method · Build an answer from evidence

nodes.label: Frame the problem
nodes.text: Use [[independent judgement]] to decide what remains unexplained.

nodes.label: Return to the evidence
nodes.text: Go back to the [[primary sources]], then develop a [[working hypothesis]] from the gaps.

nodes.label: Write and substantiate
nodes.text: Present the research in scientific papers, supporting the argument with evidence.

stages.title: Conclusion · What the learner carries forward
stages.relation: draw out the value of this education

nodes.label: The lasting value
nodes.text: [[Method]], and the capacity and drive to learn, matter more than the degree.

nodes.label: The task ahead
nodes.text: History calls for [[revision]]. Young learners can take up that task.

title: Should the Robots Be Taxed?
subtitle: A proposed tax, a historical test, and the cost of transition

stages.title: 01 · The debate and its proposed solution

nodes.label: The concern
nodes.text: If robots replace workers, governments may lose tax revenue while people face [[unemployment]].

nodes.label: The proposal
nodes.text: Tax robot owners and use a [[basic income]] to protect those whose jobs disappear.

stages.title: 02 · Put the proposal in historical context

nodes.label: Tools keep changing
nodes.text: Robots belong to a long history of [[automation]]. New tools change how people work; later generations learn new skills.

nodes.label: Work is reorganised
nodes.text: Handloom weaving gives way to factory production: fixed hours, shared machinery and a greater [[division of labour]].

nodes.label: Change extends beyond jobs
nodes.text: Birth rates fall and populations age. Future generations may learn to [[conserve resources]] as conditions change.

stages.title: 03 · Answer three objections
stages.relation: apply this history to present concerns

nodes.label: What happens to employment?
nodes.text: Some workers are left behind during the [[lag]]. Other skills and jobs emerge, but the benefits remain [[uneven]].

nodes.label: What happens to taxes?
nodes.text: Machines earn no wages, but the author argues that higher [[corporate profits]] and new robot-related jobs create other tax revenue.

nodes.label: Is the speed unprecedented?
nodes.text: Earlier transport revolutions also displaced workers. Today's rapid flow of [[information]] makes disruption more visible.

stages.title: 04 · The author's response

nodes.label: Adjustment takes time
nodes.text: A disrupted system does not reach a new [[equilibrium]] immediately. The transition can be painful.

nodes.label: Respond to people
nodes.text: The present phase calls for [[empathy]], compassion and [[social responsibility]].

title: Roommates
subtitle: Three stages of companionship lead to an inherited way of living

stages.title: 01 · Looking back

nodes.label: The unusual roommate
nodes.text: The narrator's grandfather lives to 107. For years, the grandson takes his extraordinary [[energy]] for granted.

stages.title: 02 · Childhood: hearing without understanding
stages.relation: return to the earliest shared room

nodes.label: The boy's perspective
nodes.text: The boy casts himself as his grandfather's [[teacher]], explaining electricity and other school knowledge.

nodes.label: What the older narrator now hears
nodes.text: The grandfather's quarrels and dreams once sounded like noise. In [[retrospect]], those outbursts become [[music]].

stages.title: 03 · Graduate school: closeness across difference

nodes.label: A renewed household
nodes.text: Despite the age gap, the grandson is his most [[congenial companion]]. His grandfather makes friends and does much of the housework.

nodes.label: Two ideas of work
nodes.text: Reading on a couch counts as study for the grandson; the grandfather mocks it as [[laziness]]. Their closeness does not erase misunderstanding.

stages.title: 04 · Adulthood: the direction of care reverses
stages.relation: a family crisis exposes a different kind of strength

nodes.label: An expectation overturned
nodes.text: The established grandson plans to care for his grandfather. His wife's illness creates a painful [[irony]]: he needs the help instead.

nodes.label: Two responses to suffering
nodes.text: The grandson turns anger inward as [[depression]]. His grandfather responds through the ordinary work of [[daily life]].

nodes.label: An example becomes a way back
nodes.text: Caring for children, reading the news and mowing the lawn continue. After two years, the grandson begins to [[join him]].

stages.title: 05 · Present self: carrying the example forward

nodes.label: The lasting lesson
nodes.text: The narrator now gets up early and stays [[busy]]. His final tribute expresses [[gratitude]] for a roommate whose example taught him how to keep living.

title: Never Trust Appearances
subtitle: Observation becomes assumption—until evidence breaks the pattern

stages.title: 01 · An ordinary train journey

nodes.label: James's routine
nodes.text: James takes the later train to secure his usual [[corner seat]]. He quietly reads while commuters hurry around him.

nodes.label: Matti's limited view
nodes.text: On his [[first visit]] to England, Matti studies the one passenger he can see clearly.

stages.title: 02 · Expectations filter what Matti sees
stages.relation: interpret a stranger through a ready-made image

nodes.label: The imagined Englishman
nodes.text: Matti expects a bowler hat, fair hair, a moustache and a pipe. He treats these features as signs of a [[typical Englishman]].

nodes.label: The actual passenger
nodes.text: James has dark curly hair and no hat or moustache. His [[old clothes]] and worn briefcase become Matti's evidence for an invented life.

stages.title: 03 · Details turn into an unsupported story

nodes.label: Invent an identity
nodes.text: The initials J. S. suggest “John Smith”. Matti guesses that James is a poorly paid [[clerk]], shop assistant or teacher.

nodes.label: Invent a household
nodes.text: Matti supplies a wife, an increasing number of children and a tiny garden. His [[pity]] rests on [[assumptions]], not verified facts.

stages.title: 04 · Reality overturns the reading
stages.relation: confront the imagined story with evidence

nodes.label: The visible contradiction
nodes.text: A uniformed chauffeur opens a [[Rolls-Royce]] for James. Matti's account can no longer explain what he sees.

nodes.label: Geoffrey supplies the facts
nodes.text: Sir James controls 42 factories and is a [[bachelor]]. His parents are [[Finnish]], and his real name is Jussi Saksalainen.

nodes.label: The judgement under examination
nodes.text: Matti recalls warnings about his [[unreliable imagination]]. Appearance alone cannot establish a person's identity or life.

title: Courage
subtitle: A direct proposal brings parental authority and personal choice into conflict

stages.title: 01 · An arrival that breaks convention

nodes.label: The expected route
nodes.text: Marriage negotiations would normally pass through parents and a [[go-between]].

nodes.label: Akira's chosen route
nodes.text: Akira comes [[directly]] to Chie's door on a cold, rainy evening, interrupting the warmth shared by mother and daughter.

stages.title: 02 · Politeness meets a mistaken assumption

nodes.label: A respectful visitor
nodes.text: Akira bows, apologises and speaks with [[sincerity]]. Chie begins to like him.

nodes.label: A parent's blind spot
nodes.text: His earnest speech produces [[maternal amusement]]. Chie still sees both him and Naomi as [[children]].

stages.title: 03 · One proposal, two possible homes

nodes.label: With parental consent
nodes.text: Akira will stay in [[Japan]], become Naomi's yoshi and live in the House of Fuji.

nodes.label: Without parental consent
nodes.text: His dentistry position in [[Seattle]] offers another route: he will secure a home in America for his bride.

stages.title: 04 · The proposal changes the emotional balance
stages.relation: make the possibility of separation real

nodes.label: Chie's sudden chill
nodes.text: Asked for Naomi's hand, Chie suddenly feels the night's [[dampness]]. The matter she dismissed now touches her own family.

nodes.label: Akira leaves the decision open
nodes.text: He apologises for startling her and promises to return in [[two weeks]]. No consent has yet been given.

stages.title: 05 · Mother and daughter confront the same choice

nodes.label: Chie's expectation
nodes.text: Chie dismisses Akira's hopes as [[preposterous]] and waits for Naomi to laugh with her.

nodes.label: Naomi's resolve
nodes.text: Naomi answers with [[silence]], then declares, “I mean to have him.” Her [[determination]] challenges the assumption that her mother will decide for her.

title: Reading
subtitle: Access to books → a writing problem → deliberate practice → improvement

stages.title: A reader finds ways to learn

nodes.label: Buy and exchange
nodes.text: His childhood [[bookish inclination]] leads him to spend his money on books and sell one collection to buy another.

nodes.label: Read what is available
nodes.text: His father's religious books encourage argument; Plutarch, Defoe and Mather also shape his [[thinking]].

nodes.label: Borrow beyond the home
nodes.text: Booksellers' apprentices and Matthew Adams give him access to better books, often read late into the night.

stages.title: Reading changes his direction

nodes.label: A practical occupation
nodes.text: His love of books helps determine his [[apprenticeship]] as a printer, which gives him further access to reading.

nodes.label: Two reactions to poetry
nodes.text: A ballad's sales flatter his [[vanity]], but his father ridicules the writing and discourages a poetic career.

nodes.label: A different ambition
nodes.text: He moves towards [[prose]], later an important means of his advancement.

stages.title: A dispute exposes a writing problem

nodes.label: From debate to letters
nodes.text: Unable to settle a dispute with Collins over women's education, Franklin puts his [[arguments]] into writing.

nodes.label: Accept specific criticism
nodes.text: His father praises his spelling and punctuation but finds weak expression, method and [[perspicuity]]. Franklin resolves to improve.

stages.title: The Spectator becomes a working model

nodes.label: Read → note → wait
nodes.text: He records short [[hints]] of each sentence's meaning, then puts the original aside for several days.

nodes.label: Rebuild from meaning
nodes.text: Without looking back, he [[reconstructs]] the essays in whatever words he can find.

nodes.label: Compare → correct
nodes.text: Comparison with the original reveals faults and a limited [[stock of words]], directing the next round of practice.

stages.title: Different exercises address different weaknesses

nodes.label: Word choice
nodes.text: Prose → verse → prose forces him to search for verbal [[variety]] and recall suitable alternatives.

nodes.label: Order of ideas
nodes.text: Jumbling and rearranging his notes teaches [[method]] in the arrangement of thoughts.

nodes.label: Sustained improvement
nodes.text: Practice at night, before work and on Sundays builds [[confidence]] that he can become a competent English writer.

title: What We Gain or Lose in Cities
subtitle: Urban growth → two trade-offs → the conditions behind our choices

stages.title: Cities change the setting of human life

nodes.label: Most of human history
nodes.text: People live at low densities in families and small bands.

nodes.label: The past 6,000 years
nodes.text: Cities emerge; today they house more than half the world's population.

nodes.label: The central claim
nodes.text: Urban life involves [[trade-offs]]: substantial gains can come with substantial costs.

stages.title: Trade-off 1 · Individual freedom and community interests

nodes.label: Singapore · collective security
nodes.text: High density and dependence on neighbours encourage close [[monitoring]]. Citizens accept less freedom for health, safety and high living standards.

nodes.label: Germany · shared public goods
nodes.text: Rules protect architecture, trees and fish stocks. Limits on individual choice support long-term [[community interests]].

nodes.label: Los Angeles · individual rights
nodes.text: Strong [[property rights]] allow broad personal freedom, but the resulting [[free-for-all]] harms neighbours, trees, architecture and fish populations.

stages.title: Why do these societies choose differently?

nodes.label: Geography and density
nodes.text: Land, resources and [[population density]] affect how closely one person's actions constrain others.

nodes.label: Urban history
nodes.text: Different lengths of urban experience help form distinct [[customs]].

nodes.label: Patterns of settlement
nodes.text: Communal farming, close-packed farms and scattered frontier families leave different [[cultural legacies]].

stages.title: Trade-off 2 · Social ties and anonymity

nodes.label: Village life · support and constraint
nodes.text: New Guinea villages offer lifelong friends and [[social support]]. Constant watching, demands and gossip can also become [[socially suffocating]].

nodes.label: City life · isolation and freedom
nodes.text: Scattered friendships can produce [[isolation]], but [[anonymity]] also allows privacy, peaceful solitude and freedom from constant clan demands.

stages.title: A choice of compromises

nodes.label: The question remains open
nodes.text: As urbanisation increases, which [[compromises]] would we accept for safety, health, prosperity and attractive surroundings?

title: The Guide to Being a Foodie Without Being Culturally Appropriative
subtitle: A personal contradiction → unequal power → mechanisms → consequences → response

stages.title: An everyday contradiction raises the question

nodes.label: The food of childhood
nodes.text: Foods from the author's culture are mocked as strange or presented as an [[exotic]] spectacle.

nodes.label: The fashionable version
nodes.text: The same foods become expensive restaurant [[trends]], while their communities still face prejudice.

stages.title: Where does enjoyment become appropriation?

nodes.label: Cross-cultural enjoyment
nodes.text: Trying, cooking and enjoying another culture's food are not automatically [[appropriation]].

nodes.label: An unequal relationship
nodes.text: The author's concern is a [[dominant culture]] extracting pleasure, profit or control from communities it has oppressed.

stages.title: Three mechanisms of appropriation

nodes.label: Culture as spectacle
nodes.text: [[Fetishization]] turns people and histories into exotic dishes and a fixed idea of “authentic” culture.

nodes.label: Culture as a product
nodes.text: [[Commercialization]] repackages community food for outside consumption and profit.

nodes.label: Control over resources
nodes.text: [[Access hoarding]] lets dominant groups control the ingredients and resources needed to produce the food.

stages.title: What gets lost when food is detached from people?

nodes.label: Cultural flattening
nodes.text: Reducing Japan to sushi or India to curry encourages [[homogenization]] and erases diverse communities and histories.

nodes.label: Disconnection
nodes.text: Enjoying selected dishes while ignoring [[oppression]] separates food from colonial histories, labour rights and current community concerns.

nodes.label: Loss of access
nodes.text: Food [[gentrification]] can make traditional ingredients and cuisines unaffordable to their own communities.

stages.title: Enjoy food with attention to people and power

nodes.label: Ask who benefits
nodes.text: Consider who is [[labouring and profiting]], where recipes come from, and whose access is being reduced.

nodes.label: Learn beyond the menu
nodes.text: Keep enjoying food across cultures while learning about [[colonization]] and the issues affecting the communities behind it.

title: Stop Telling Me to Travel like a Local, Okay?
subtitle: Own the tourist identity → challenge the myth → learn openly → bring curiosity home

stages.title: The author's starting position

nodes.label: A self-aware visitor
nodes.text: She accepts being a [[cultural interloper]], uses experienced travellers' and locals' knowledge, and seeks a place's “only-here” highlights.

stages.title: Test the promise of “travel like a local”

nodes.label: The advertised promise
nodes.text: Insider tips offer an [[inside scoop]] while tourist-shaming urges visitors to hide their unfamiliarity.

nodes.label: The everyday reality
nodes.text: Locals work, commute and do chores. Travelling like them is a [[contradiction]] when a holiday aims to escape routine.

nodes.label: The tourist's opportunity
nodes.text: Museums, special meals and wandering with [[fresh eyes]] are distinctive pleasures of being a visitor.

stages.title: Admitting unfamiliarity opens a path to learning

nodes.label: Acknowledge what you lack
nodes.text: Accept [[ignorance]] and [[vulnerability]] instead of pretending to understand everything already.

nodes.label: Learn from others
nodes.text: Cooking classes, guided market visits and local [[expertise]] explain practices a visitor cannot simply intuit.

nodes.label: Receive unexpected kindness
nodes.text: Experiences in Thailand, Kyoto and Paris show how openness can invite [[hospitality]] and personal connection.

stages.title: Freedom from fitting in still allows respect

nodes.label: Release social anxiety
nodes.text: Travel's [[anonymity]] frees visitors to look unfamiliar, ask directions and stop worrying about appearances.

nodes.label: Keep cultural consideration
nodes.text: This freedom still requires respecting local [[customs]], including religious and cultural expectations about dress.

stages.title: Bring the tourist's attention into everyday life

nodes.label: Familiarity can postpone action
nodes.text: Assuming nearby places will always be there produces [[apathy]] and repeated delay.

nodes.label: Visit, notice and participate
nodes.text: [[Tourist energy]] restores curiosity and urgency: take the tour, enter the museum and explore the places close to home.

title: Two Ways of Seeing a River
subtitle: One river, two readings → professional knowledge → the question of gain and loss

stages.title: The river is a book that different readers see differently

nodes.label: The passenger's eye
nodes.text: The water is a [[dead language]]: its surface offers attractive pictures, while a faint dimple may seem insignificant.

nodes.label: The trained pilot's eye
nodes.text: The river tells a new story every day. The same dimple is a warning of a hidden [[wreck or rock]].

stages.title: The same sunset · beauty becomes information

nodes.label: BEFORE · colours and shapes
nodes.text: Red water brightens into gold, a black log stands out, and a slanting mark [[sparkles]] on the surface.

nodes.label: AFTER · weather and danger
nodes.text: The sunset means wind; the log signals a [[rising river]]; the slanting mark reveals a dangerous [[reef]].

stages.title: The same water · attractive patterns become warnings

nodes.label: BEFORE · a scene of wonder
nodes.text: Tumbling rings shine like an [[opal]], circles trace delicate patterns, and a trail glows silver in the forest's shadow.

nodes.label: AFTER · a changing channel
nodes.text: The rings reveal a dissolving bar; the circles mean dangerous [[shoaling]]; the silver streak exposes a new [[snag]].

stages.title: A change in attention changes the river's value

nodes.label: The enchanted view
nodes.text: A leafy bough glows like flame above the forest. The novice takes in the whole scene with speechless [[rapture]].

nodes.label: The professional view
nodes.text: The same dying tree is a night-time [[landmark]] that may soon disappear. Features now matter for safe navigation, and their beauty gradually goes unnoticed.

stages.title: Beyond the river · an unresolved question

nodes.label: The doctor analogy
nodes.text: A lovely flush may suggest [[disease]] to a doctor: professional interpretation can displace admiration.

nodes.label: Weigh acquisition against loss
nodes.text: Has learning a trade brought more [[gain or loss]]? Twain leaves the reader to consider both knowledge acquired and wonder diminished.
